Load a week

Use a week like yours, or any week. Nothing is saved. Open a category, read what the research says, and add blocks. On the ride, steer into greens and around reds and frayed bands. The panel below shows what this week will change.

How the ride works
You ride one fiber in a circuit. After a bad, the thorny alarm fibers fire harder. After a green, the thinking fibers light up and grow new tips.
Frayed bands (striped, loose fibers) slow you down.
Bads: frayed bands get wider and you slow. Hit three and the signal fades.
Greens: steer into them. Frayed bands get narrower. They do not change your speed.
Yellow double rings are checkpoints.
At each gap, match the shape: steer onto the spine whose receptor matches the messenger in the center before its ring closes. Two good landings fire the next neuron. Too few and it costs a hit.

What you are

You are a signal riding a nerve fiber. Real signals do not swerve; steering is the game's way of letting you ride one. The ride follows a touch from your fingertip: three neurons carry it to your sensory cortex, then one more hop reaches the thinking cortex.

What you will see

  • Bright rings: gaps in the insulation (nodes). The signal leaps from node to node, which is why it is fast.
  • Frayed bands: damaged insulation, drawn as amber stripes with loose fibers at the edges. They slow you, and hitting one counts as a hit.
  • Red cubes (rough edges) are bads: a short night, a test, a phone at 2 a.m. Every bad that pops up or that you hit makes the frayed bands wider and slows you. Three hits and the signal fades; you go back to the last checkpoint.
  • Green cubes (rounded) are goods: sleep, a walk, a friend, a meal, practice. Steer into a green and the frayed bands get narrower. Nothing in the ride speeds you up; the bright rings show the signal leaping, at a steady speed.
  • Yellow double rings: checkpoints, halfway through each leg and at each relay.
  • The end of each fiber: a gap, then the next neuron's landing spines. Line up with a lit spine to land.
  • Before each ride you load a week onto the balance. Every card in the deck: short night, test tomorrow, phone at 2 a.m., missed bus, loud room (stress); real sleep, a walk, a friend, a good meal, practice (support). Each card you load shows up as a picture during the ride. Choose the calm road to ride with no week.
  • The week changes the last relay, in the thinking cortex: stress cubes take landing spines away and strengthen the survival shortcut's pull; support cubes add spines back; practice moves the balance point so stress tips it less. The first three relays carry the touch the same either way, because stress does not stop you feeling a touch.

What's happening here

A long stretch of short nights thins the landing spines in the thinking cortex, and the alarm circuits get stronger. That is the body protecting you, not failing. In animal studies, thinned spines grew back once the stress eased. Pad counts in the game are a simplified picture; most of this evidence comes from rats.

Sources

  • OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e, Ch. 12 (CC BY 4.0): conduction speed, myelin, nodes, synapses.
  • Arnsten, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2009: stress, prefrontal spines, amygdala.
  • Radley et al., 2005 and 2006: spine loss after repeated stress, and recovery.
  • The Resilience Balance, as taught in MassBay's Toolkit of Trauma-Informed Pedagogies & Practices, after the Alberta Family Wellness Initiative's Resilience Scale.
  • Tube and objects: studio drawings in the style of Brainbow imaging (Livet et al., 2007).

The week: research behind each block

  • Short nights (stress, weight 2): After a night without sleep, the brain's alarm center reacted over 60% more strongly to upsetting pictures. (Yoo et al., 2007, Current Biology)
  • Phone in bed (stress, weight 1): Reading on a lit screen before bed delayed sleep and the sleep hormone melatonin, compared with a printed book. (Chang et al., 2015, PNAS)
  • Test tomorrow (stress, weight 1): Short stress can take the brain's planning center offline within minutes. It comes back when the stress passes. (Arnsten, 2009, Nature Reviews Neuroscience)
  • Deadlines piling up (stress, weight 2): Stress that feels out of your control hits harder. A sense of control lets the planning center calm the alarm. (Maier and Seligman, 2016, Psychological Review)
  • Skipped meals (stress, weight 2): In a national survey of about 86,000 students, 48% at two-year colleges had faced food insecurity in the past 30 days. (Hope Center #RealCollege report, 2019)
  • Rent due (stress, weight 2): In the Hope Center's national survey, 60% of two-year college students had faced housing insecurity in the past year. (Hope Center #RealCollege report, 2019)
  • Shift before class (stress, weight 1): In 2020, 40% of full-time and 74% of part-time undergraduates were working while enrolled. (National Center for Education Statistics, 2022)
  • Missed the bus (stress, weight 1): A surprise you cannot control is the kind of stress that lands hardest; predictable stress is easier to absorb. (Maier and Seligman, 2016, Psychological Review)
  • Loud, crowded room (stress, weight 1): Children at schools under flight paths read worse the louder the aircraft noise. (Stansfeld et al., 2005, The Lancet (RANCH study))
  • Feeling alone (stress, weight 2): Across 148 studies, people with stronger social ties had 50% better odds of survival over the study periods. (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010, PLOS Medicine)
  • A full night of sleep (builder, weight 2): Adults need 7 or more hours a night. About a third of U.S. adults get less. (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
  • A walk or workout (builder, weight 1): Exercise raises BDNF, a protein that helps new connections between neurons grow. (van Praag; reviewed in Liu and Nusslock, 2018, Frontiers in Neuroscience)
  • A friend who listens (builder, weight 2): In a lab stress test, men who had their best friend with them beforehand had lower stress-hormone (cortisol) responses. (Heinrichs et al., 2003, Biological Psychiatry)
  • A professor who cares (builder, weight 1): Graduates who had a professor who cared, one who made them excited to learn, and a mentor had more than double the odds of being engaged at work. (Gallup-Purdue Index, 2014)
  • Practice (builder, weight 1): Skills and abilities set the balance point: with more skill, the same weight tips the scale less. (Alberta Family Wellness Initiative, Resilience Scale)
  • Slow breathing (builder, weight 1): Breathing slowly, about six breaths a minute, raises heart-rate variability, a sign the body's calming system is working. (Zaccaro et al., 2018, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience)
  • An if-then plan (builder, weight 1): Across 94 studies, if-then plans ("If it's 7 p.m., then I start the essay") helped people reach goals, a medium-to-large effect. (Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology)
  • Time outside (builder, weight 1): People who spent at least 120 minutes a week in nature were more likely to report good health and well-being. (White et al., 2019, Scientific Reports)
  • A group where you belong (builder, weight 1): A one-hour activity showing new students that worries about belonging are common and fade raised Black students' grades over three years. (Walton and Cohen, 2011, Science)
  • Campus food pantry (builder, weight 1): Basic-needs gaps are common (48% food insecurity at two-year colleges), so campuses run pantries and emergency aid. Using them is support, not failure. (Hope Center #RealCollege report, 2019)
  • Weights are a studio simplification: long-running loads, basic needs, isolation, full sleep and close friends weigh 2; single events weigh 1. After the Harvard Center on the Developing Child: duration and support decide how hard stress lands.

Outside the tube

You are riding one fiber in a circuit. The fibers beside you belong to neighboring neurons, joined at cell bodies and cross-links. The racing lights are signals moving through that circuit; when a signal reaches a cell body it can jump across a link to the next fiber. Behind the circuit, dimmed, are Santiago Ramón y Cajal's ink drawings of the region you are in; flashes of lightning light up parts of them.

What the lights mean

  • After a bad: a pink-red wave runs along the circuit. The two thorny alarm fibers fire harder and grow spiky cell bodies, and the other fibers dim. Stress chemicals strengthen the brain's alarm circuits and weaken connections in the thinking cortex for a while (Arnsten, 2009).
  • After a green: a green wave runs along the circuit. The thinking fibers brighten, signals pick up, and the cell bodies grow new green tips that stay as you ride past. Sleep, movement and support help connections relight and new spines grow back (Radley et al., 2005; exercise raises BDNF).
  • The more bads you are carrying, the louder the alarm fibers and the redder the lightning. This is a studio picture of the research, not a picture of your brain.

Where to go

If something here brought up something hard, you can call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, US) any time.

The signal faded

Three hits. What's happening here: damaged insulation can stop a signal. Each hard thing widened the frayed bands until there was almost no clear path left. Greens narrow them again.

You reached the thinking cortex

Words for what you felt

  • Saltatory conduction: the signal leaps node to node along the insulated fiber.
  • Synapse: the gap between neurons, where the signal lands on the next neuron.
  • Dendritic spines: the landing places on the next neuron.
